# The University–Contractor–State Triangle {#sec-3-11}

::: {.chapter-meta}
Act II — Hoover, War, and the Archive State · 1942–1945
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="draft"}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Pre-Draft Brief

**Core question.** Why does federal money route through universities?

**The answer.** Because universities supply the two things the state cannot buy
directly: talent and legitimacy. Contractors provide production, the state
provides demand and classification, and the university provides people and the
appearance of disinterest. California received disproportionate federal research
money because it was the only place hosting all three layers in one metropolitan
area.

**The mechanism.** Public subsidy converted into private monopoly, with the
triangle specified. This is the book's structural centre for the twentieth
century, and the chapter should be diagrammatic in its clarity: three parties,
three contributions, and a flow of public money that ends in private balance
sheets.

**The key fact.** The institutional architecture of Silicon Valley was built in
procurement offices, not garages. The garage is the story the system tells about
itself; the contract file is what actually happened.

**The human anchor.** A contracting officer. The least glamorous figure in the
book and one of the most consequential — the person whose signature determines
which region gets an industry.

**Excluded voices.** The taxpayer, structurally: funding research whose results
are classified and whose commercial value accrues to private firms. And the
legislature, which appropriates in aggregate and cannot see the allocation.

**Proof.** This chapter proves that federal money routed through universities
because universities laundered its legitimacy by showing what each of the three
parties contributed and what each extracted.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Working summary

The founding document of Silicon Valley is a contract file, and this chapter
opens on it rather than on a garage.

Its argument is schematic, and deliberately so: three parties, three
contributions, one flow of public money. The state supplies demand and
classification. Contractors supply production. Universities supply talent and,
more valuably, legitimacy. Each party gets something it cannot obtain elsewhere,
and the arrangement is stable because all three have an interest in its
continuation.

The interesting question is why the money routes through universities at all,
and the chapter gives two answers. The state cannot fund firms directly at this
scale without the appearance of favouritism, and a university's disinterest is
an asset worth paying for. And it cannot do the work in-house because civil
service salaries and hiring timelines cannot compete for the people it needs.

The unglamorous heart of the chapter is indirect cost recovery. Overhead — the
percentage of every research grant that goes to the institution rather than the
project — is the university's actual revenue model, and following it explains
far more about institutional behaviour than any statement of academic mission.
Universities compete for grants because grants are income, and the income
arrives whether or not the research succeeds.

Classification is what makes the arrangement unaccountable. The public funds
research it is not permitted to read, and the commercial value of the results
accrues to private firms. The taxpayer and the legislature are structurally
excluded — the legislature appropriates in aggregate and cannot see the
allocation.

California ended up with a disproportionate share because it hosted all three
layers in one metropolitan area: Moffett Field and the aviation industry, the
Pacific theatre, and two major research universities within forty miles of each
other.

This diagram is the machine. Every subsequent chapter in this book is the same
triangle with different company names in the second box.
:::

## Beats

1. **Hook.** A contract file. Open on the document that the garage story exists
   to obscure.
2. **The three layers.** University, contractor, state. What each supplies and
   what each receives. Keep it schematic and short; the reader should be able to
   redraw it from memory.
3. **Why not fund firms directly.** The legitimacy problem. A university's
   disinterest is an asset the state is willing to pay for.
4. **Why not do it in-house.** Civil service constraints, salaries, and the
   speed of academic hiring.
5. **Overhead.** The unglamorous heart of the chapter: indirect cost recovery as
   the university's actual revenue model. Follow the money to where it lands.
6. **Classification.** What secrecy does to accountability. The public cannot
   audit what it cannot read.
7. **California's concentration.** Why the three layers ended up adjacent here
   rather than elsewhere. Specific: Moffett, the aviation industry, the Pacific
   theatre, Stanford and Berkeley.
8. **The excluded.** The taxpayer and the legislature, structurally rather than
   rhetorically.
9. **Landing.** The triangle is the machine. Every subsequent chapter in the
   book is this diagram with different company names in the second box.

::: {.chapter-question}
Why does federal money route through universities?
:::

The founding document of Silicon Valley is a contract file.

Not a garage, not a schematic, and not a napkin. A file: a solicitation, a
proposal, a negotiated agreement, a schedule of deliverables, a security
classification, and an overhead rate. Thousands of them, running from federal
agencies through universities and into companies, from 1945 onward, without
interruption.

This chapter is the diagram, and it is deliberately schematic, because the
reader should be able to redraw it from memory for the remaining two acts.

## Three parties

The **state** supplies demand and classification. It decides what problems are
worth money, how much, and who may see the results. Its demand is not price-
sensitive in the ordinary way, because the buyer is not trying to make a profit
on the purchase, and it is durable, because strategic competition does not end.

The **contractor** supplies production. It manufactures, it scales, and it takes
the commercial risk. It also employs people at salaries and on timescales that
no government department could match.

The **university** supplies two things. The obvious one is talent: graduates,
doctoral students, and faculty who know the science. The less obvious one is
legitimacy, and it is worth more.

## Why the legitimacy matters

Ask why the money routes through universities at all, and the answers are more
interesting than they first appear.

The government could fund companies directly, and does. But direct payments from
a federal agency to private firms for research whose commercial benefits the
firms will keep is politically awkward, and it looks like what it is. Routing
the work through a university transforms the transaction. A university is
disinterested, or is understood to be. It has no shareholders. Its output is
knowledge, which is a public good. Money that goes to a university is an
investment in national capability; the identical money paid to a corporation is
a subsidy.

The government also cannot do the work in-house at the necessary scale, and the
reasons are mundane and decisive: civil service pay scales cannot compete for
senior scientists, hiring timelines are measured in months, and a federal
laboratory cannot easily be closed when the field moves.

So the university sits in the middle, and what it is actually supplying — beyond
the science, which is real — is the appearance of public purpose over a flow of
funds whose eventual commercial beneficiaries are private.

## Overhead

The unglamorous heart of the arrangement is indirect cost recovery, and
following it explains institutional behaviour better than any statement of
academic mission.

A research grant has two components. Direct costs pay for the work: salaries,
equipment, materials. Indirect costs — overhead — are a negotiated percentage
added on top, nominally to cover the institution's share of buildings,
utilities, administration, and libraries.

That percentage is substantial. Rates at major American research universities
have run for decades at levels that add a very large fraction to every grant,
and the money is fungible: it goes to the institution, not to the project.

The consequences are structural. A university's incentive is to maximise grant
volume, because grant volume is income. Departments that attract funding grow,
and departments that do not, do not. Faculty are evaluated substantially on the
money they bring in. And the income arrives whether or not the research
succeeds, because overhead is charged on expenditure rather than on results.

None of this is corrupt and all of it shapes behaviour. When Terman said the
university should build steeples in fields where federal money was going, he was
describing a revenue strategy in the vocabulary of academic excellence, and both
descriptions were accurate.

## Classification

Secrecy is what makes the arrangement unaccountable, and the chapter should be
plain about the mechanics.

Classified research cannot be published, discussed with uncleared colleagues, or
examined by anyone outside the system. A legislator votes on an appropriation in
aggregate and cannot see the allocation. A taxpayer funds work whose existence
may itself be classified. A journalist has nothing to read.

The people in a position to evaluate whether the money is well spent are the
people receiving it and the agency officials who allocated it, and both have an
interest in the answer being yes.

## Why California

The three layers ended up adjacent on the San Francisco Peninsula, and the
reasons are specific rather than mystical.

Moffett Field in Sunnyvale had been an aeronautical facility since the 1930s and
became the Ames Aeronautical Laboratory, later NASA Ames. The Pacific theatre
had made the west coast strategically central and left installations behind. The
aircraft industry in southern California had produced an enormous manufacturing
base and a supply chain. Stanford and Berkeley were within forty miles of each
other, and both were building research capacity aggressively with federal money.

And by the early 1950s a university with eight thousand acres began leasing land
to firms that wanted to be near all of it.

Nowhere else in the United States had every element in one metropolitan area.
Boston had universities and contractors but no equivalent concentration of
aerospace manufacturing or federal installations. Southern California had
manufacturing and installations but its universities were not yet organised the
way Terman was organising his.

## Who owns the result

One question was left unresolved for thirty-five years, and its resolution in
1980 is the subject of a chapter in the next act. It is worth stating here,
because it is the hole in the diagram.

If the public pays for research and a university performs it, who owns the
invention?

Before 1980 the answer was messy and varied by agency. The default position in
much of the federal government was that inventions made with public money
belonged to the public, and agencies either took title themselves or licensed
non-exclusively to anyone who wanted a licence. The consequence, its critics
argued, was that a great deal of federally funded research was never
commercialised at all, because no firm would invest in developing a product it
could not protect.

That argument has real force and the chapter concedes it. A patent that anyone
may practise is a patent nobody will invest behind.

The counter-argument has equal force and is less often stated. Exclusive
licensing of publicly funded research means the public pays twice — once for the
research through taxes, and once for the product at a monopoly price — and the
university takes a royalty in the middle.

For the period this chapter describes, the question sits unresolved and the
money flows anyway, because the immediate commercial applications of most
defence research were limited and the firms doing the development were the same
firms holding the contracts. It becomes urgent when the research starts
producing recombinant DNA and search algorithms, and Act III chapter 10 is where
it is settled.

## The excluded

The taxpayer and the legislature, structurally rather than rhetorically.

The taxpayer funds research, cannot examine it, and does not share in the
commercial returns when the results are eventually commercialised — a gap that
Bayh-Dole in 1980 will widen considerably, as Act III chapter 10 describes.

The legislature appropriates in aggregate and cannot see where the money lands.
It can cut a programme; it cannot audit an allocation that is classified.

This is not an argument that the arrangement was wrong. It produced the
transistor's commercialisation, the internet, satellite navigation, and much
else, and the returns to the public from that portfolio are enormous even
allowing for everything this book says about who captured the surplus.

It is an argument that the arrangement was never chosen, in the sense of being
debated and approved. It was assembled, in wartime, for wartime reasons, and
then it stayed.

Every subsequent chapter of this book is this diagram with different names in
the second box. Fairchild, Lockheed, Intel, Netscape, Palantir, and a company
that sells accelerators for training language models: the university and the
state are constant, and the contractor changes.
